Abstract This study aims to chart the development and thematic contours of cash waqf research within Islamic finance through an integrated bibliometric approach. Cash waqf or monetary endowments governed by Shariah law has attracted increasing scholarly and practical interest for its capacity to support socio-economic initiatives. We collected 381 records from Scopus and Web of Science, which, after deduplication and quality checks, resulted in 237 publications for analysis using ScientoPy and VOSviewer. Descriptive statistics revealed a three-fold rise in annual outputs between 2014 and 2024, with Malaysia and Indonesia leading contributions. Co-citation and keyword co-occurrence mapping uncovered four central research themes: institutional financial sustainability, digital and fintech integration, regulatory frameworks, and measurement of social impact. Network analysis highlighted prolific authors and key journals driving the discourse. The results indicate rapid diversification in cash waqf scholarship, with growing emphasis on technology enabled solutions and enhanced governance. Findings underscore strategic areas for future study such as policy harmonization, blockchain applications, and international collaboration that can refine implementation practices and amplify the impact of cash waqf mechanisms in Islamic finance. Keywords: waqf fund, cash endowment, scientometric, web of science, scopus 1. Introduction The notion of cash waqf is getting more recognition lately due to its potential to propel positive economic empowerment within the framework of Islamic finance (Syathiri, 2025). The concept of cash waqf has progressed to a critical financial instrument within the framework of Islamic finance (Baryal et al., 2022; Islam, 2015), contributing to an increase number of sustainable solutions aimed at socio-economic development (Akhter et al., 2025; Asni et al., 2024; Hasbulah et al., 2024; Noor et al., 2024). Unlike traditional waqf, which predominantly involves fixed assets, cash waqf offers greater flexibility in the mobilization of resources for public welfare initiatives (Aldeen et al., 2022). It sets itself as a crucial part in financing education, healthcare, and poverty alleviation while complying with the Shariah principles (Kachkar & Alfares, 2022). Over time, researchers have discovered various aspects of cash waqf, scrutinising its economic impact, governance structures, and potential integration with modern financial technologies (Hasbulah et al., 2024). Due to the popularity and the demands of cash waqf, it is vital to evaluate research trends and advances in this domain in order to comprehend both its present and future potential and usage. In spite of the surge of the literature on cash waqf, some aspects of cash waqf remain underexplored. Existing studies have mostly focused on theoretical frameworks and historical evolution, yet there is a necessity for more empirical investigations into its real-world applications and its effectiveness in contemporary financial systems. Furthermore, while some scholars have studied the digital transformation in cash waqf management (Zakariyah et al., 2023), the wider implications of blockchain (Gazali & Ismail, 2019), artificial intelligence (Sayari, 2022), and crowd-funding in cash waqf remain unsatisfactorily addressed (Hasbulah et al., 2023). Furthermore, inconsistencies in regulatory frameworks across different jurisdictions add to the challenges in standardizing cash waqf practices, creating a gap that requires further scholarly attention. To address these gaps, this study employs bibliometric analysis to systematically review and map research developments in cash waqf. The objective is to identify dominant themes, key contributors, and influential publications shaping this field. Specifically, this study seeks to answer several research questions and motivations behind each question as follows (Table 1). Through an inclusive bibliometric analysis, this article will offer valuable understandings into the academic landscape of cash waqf research. By researching these trends, researchers and practitioners are able to identify emerging areas of interest. Moreover, this study provides policymakers with a better understanding of how cash waqf can be used to augment socio- Multidiscip. Rev. Materials and Methods 2.1. Bibliometric analysis Bibliometric analysis is an approach to examining the bibliographic characteristics of an assortment of scholarly works quantitatively. It evaluates the impact of a research by evaluating the publication metrics, citation trends, and keyword co- occurrences (Abdullah & Sofyan, 2023; Donthu et al., 2021). It involves a collection of data on publications, citations, and co- citations within a specific research field, then combined with the application of statistical techniques in order to interpret the findings (Zupic & Cater, 2015). The increase in the popularity of bibliometric analysis in numerous disciplines, including but not limited to business and management research, comes from its capacity to provide valuable insights into the evolution and structure of a research domain (Linnenluecke et al., 2020; Merigo et al., 2020). 2.2. Dataset retrieval and analysis The data for this study are collected from two well-known bibliographic repositories: Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). These databases are often utilized in bibliometric research because of their extensive and diverse academic coverage across multiple fields (Abdullah, 2022; Hafiar et al., 2024; Pranckute, 2021). The search query directed various keywords related to cash waqf in Islamic finance, such as "cash waqf" OR "fund* waqf" OR "waqf fund*" OR "cash endowment*" OR "Islamic endowment*" AND "finance*" OR "bank*" OR "commerce*" OR "invest*" OR "business." The dataset search, which are concentrated on the titles, abstracts, and keywords, is finalized on February 25th, 2025. Initially, the dataset included 381 articles, 244 from Scopus and 137 from WoS. These datasets are then further scrutinised with ScientoPy and VOSviewer, two widely-used tools in bibliometric research (Abdullah & Sofyan, 2023; Munoz et al., 2020; Rosero et al., 2019). Combining and cleaning duplicates A common occurrence in any bibliometric research is the amount of duplicate records, which often arises from the variations in the indexing practices, differences in how author names are recorded, and inconsistencies in the publication details. The removal of these redundancies is critical in maintaining the study's accuracy and reliability (Donthu et al., 2021; Linnenluecke et al., 2020). Therefore, ScientoPy is employed to merge the datasets from Scopus and WoS and to thoroughly eliminate duplicate entries which involved the comparison of key attributes such as titles, author listings, publication years, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Hasbulah et al. (2026) 3 and DOIs, which then allowed for the effective identification and removal of repeated records (Munoz et al., 2020). By addressing these duplicates, the study attains a more accurate and trustworthy reflection of the research landscape for cash waqf in Islamic finance. 2.4. General overview and of the processed bibliographic datasets The first search query in Scopus and WoS yielded publications, with 244 (64.04%) from Scopus and 137 (35.96%) from WoS. 45 publications (11.8%) are excluded on the basis of document-type criteria in order to prioritize relevant scholarly works. In this study, articles, reviews, proceedings, and conference papers are the go-to documents to be further investigated. After excluding irrelevant documents, the dataset consisted of 336 publications. Of these, 200 (59.5%) were from Scopus, and 136 (40.5%) were from WoS. Most of the dataset consisted of articles for 54.5% from Scopus and 34.8% from WoS. Reviews paper constituted 4.8% of the dataset, whereas proceedings papers comprised 3.6%, all sourced from WoS. The procedure for removing duplicates detected 99 duplicate papers for 29.5% of the papers included in both databases. Owing to duplication, Scopus eliminated 98 papers for 49% of the total. Moreover, the same reason led to the deletion of 1 paper, or 0.7% of the total papers, from WoS. Notably, 74 (74.7%) of the replicated texts exhibited disparate citation counts in the two databases. After eliminating duplicate entries, the final dataset comprised 237 papers, with 135 (57%) sourced from WoS and 102 (43%) from Scopus. Discussion An examination of the bibliometric data on cash waqf in Islamic finance research reveals a substantial increase in publications over the previous thirty years, particularly in the last eleven years. Data from Scopus and WoS indicate a consistent increase in research production, which began in 2014 (Figure 2). Multiple sources contribute to growth, such as interest in cash waqf as a topic, potentially driven by its relevance to sustainable development goals, financial inclusion, and economic empowerment within Islamic communities. During this period, scholars and practitioners may have explored new frameworks and models for utilizing cash waqf in addressing socio-economic challenges (Ascarya et al., 2023; Gazali & Che Ismail, 2019; Muhammad & Rahman, 2023; Syathiri, 2025). After analysing the top ten scientific publications contributing to cash waqf in Islamic finance research (as shown in Figure 3), it becomes clear that specialist journals hold a significant position. ISRA International Journal of Islamic Finance is the primary publication outlet, with the Journal of Islamic Accounting and Business Research being the second most prominent. These publications specifically emphasize Islamic finance and are well regarded within the discipline. They play a crucial role in sharing research findings and promoting knowledge advancement. The inclusion of other prominent publications, such as “International Journal of Islamic and Middle Eastern Finance and Management,” “Journal of Islamic Marketing,” and “Journal of King Abdul Aziz University, Islamic Economics,” highlights the increasing significance and attention given to research on cash waqf within the broader fields of Islamic finance (Alshater et al., 2021; Kahf & Mohomed, 2017; Musari, 2022). The allocation of research among these specialized publications demonstrates the advancement of the discipline and the acknowledgment of cash waqf in Islamic finance as a separate and well-defined area of research (Alshater et al., 2021; Ninglasari, 2021; Syathiri, 2025; Timur et al., 2025). Figure 4 examines the top ten institutions that have significantly contributed to cash waqf in Islamic finance research. This analysis emphasizes the notable contributions of universities from Malaysia, Indonesia and Turkey. We identified International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) as the top institution, closely followed by University Malaya (UM), Malaysia and Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM), Malaysia. These institutions are committed to promoting cash waqf in Islamic finance research through regular research production and partnerships with top institutions. Several aspects, including their specialized knowledge in Islamic finance especially in cash waqf, robust research infrastructure, and partnerships with industry stakeholders, contribute to the significance of these schools (Anam et al., 2022; Firdaus & Rizal, 2021; Misbah et al., 2022; Rusydiana et al., 2021). The inclusion of institutions from Indonesia and Turkey highlights the global scope of research in cash waqf in Islamic finance and emphasizes the importance of international collaboration in improving knowledge in this domain. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Hasbulah et al. Final Considerations The study indicates that there is a recent increase in the research interest in cash waqf in Islamic finance, from 2014 until 2024, as shown by the patterns of publication growth. The study acknowledged crucial scientific journals, research domains, highly cited publications, and institutions that have meaningfully contributed to the advancement of knowledge and practices in cash waqf for Islamic finance. However, simple publication rates are not a reliable indicator of the quality or impact of research in a specific field. Therefore, it is crucial to methodically appraise the content and the impact of research articles in all fields of study. The ongoing bibliometric analysis of cash waqf in Islamic finance has advanced this sector’s current understanding and approaches and is used to determine the primary topics, authors, and publications related to cash waqf in Islamic finance while calculating the impact and sway of research in this field. The findings of this study suggest a growing scholarly interest in investigating this subject. The study has also emphasised noteworthy scientific papers and research fields in the field of Islamic finance; in term of cash waqf in which access to this material is vital in order for professionals and researchers to be able to be updated with the latest trends in research the ability to categorize areas that require further research into. Furthermore, the study has compiled a comprehensive list of highly cited publications that have directly contributed to the increase of knowledge and practices in cash waqf for Islamic finance. Additionally, the study’s appraisal of the research output for the cash waqf-related institutes is essential in identifying the institutions that have made significant contributions to the field for which the usage of this information will be crucial for politicians, funders, and academics to determine the best distribution of resources and financing. This bibliometric study has provided many insights into the research patterns, influential scientific journals, significant research areas, highly cited publications, and institutional research outputs. Ultimately, these can offer valuable directions for future research efforts, policy-making procedures, and practical measures to improve the growth of cash waqf in the Islamic finance environment. A fundamental limitation of the study is that it is too dependent on a limited set of databases, specifically the Scopus and WoS, which may not contain all the articles on cash waqf in Islamic finance. JSON: Name: cash_waqf_bibliometric_pipeline Title: Integrated multi-database bibliometric-network analysis with dynamic topic modeling to detect emerging themes and gaps in cash waqf research Short Hypothesis: An integrated multi-database bibliometric pipeline combining Scopus and Web of Science with co-citation/co-occurrence network analysis and dynamic topic modeling will identify at least 30% more distinct emergent research themes in cash waqf literature (2014–2024) than a baseline pipeline using Scopus-only keyword co-occurrence mapping. Related Work: Existing bibliometric studies of waqf and cash waqf typically rely on single-source datasets (commonly Scopus or Web of Science) and visualization tools such as VOSviewer or basic co-occurrence counting. Prior approaches emphasize descriptive statistics (publication counts, top journals, top authors) and static network visualizations (co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence). Limitations of current methods include: dependence on one database which introduces coverage bias; limited integration of complementary techniques (for example, few studies combine co-citation networks with dynamic topic modeling); lack of reproducible, end-to-end pipelines that include deduplication, name disambiguation, and sensitivity analysis; minimal quantification of 'emergent' themes and absence of systematic validation against expert judgments; and scarce ablation or robustness testing to show how results change with database choice, deduplication strategy, or analytic thresholds. These weaknesses reduce confidence in claims about novel or emerging topics and hinder cross-study comparability. Abstract: This project develops and evaluates an integrated bibliometric research pipeline that combines multi-database retrieval (Scopus + Web of Science), rigorous deduplication and author-disambiguation, co-citation and keyword co-occurrence network analysis, and dynamic topic modeling to detect emerging themes and structural gaps in cash waqf research. The pipeline operationalizes an explicit definition of 'emergent theme' and quantifies thematic discovery performance relative to common baseline workflows (Scopus-only co-occurrence). Main contributions are: (1) a reproducible end-to-end pipeline for combining databases and generating temporally-resolved topic maps, (2) an evaluation framework that measures emergent-theme yield, topic coherence, and stability, and (3) an empirical assessment on the cash waqf corpus (1992–2025) demonstrating improved detection of understudied but rising topics such as fintech integration and regulatory harmonization. Expected outcomes include a validated methodological toolkit for researchers and policymakers and a prioritized list of robust emergent topics to inform future empirical and policy research. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Scopus records retrieved with query: ("cash waqf" OR "fund* waqf" OR "waqf fund*" OR "cash endowment*" OR "Islamic endowment*") AND (finance* OR bank* OR commerce* OR invest* OR business) limited to title/abstract/keywords, cutoff 25-Feb-2025; (B) Web of Science records with same query and cutoff. Merge and deduplicate using ScientoPy deduplication (compare title, authors, year, DOI) producing final deduped corpus (expected n=237). Baselines: Baseline 1 = Scopus-only keyword co-occurrence mapping (VOSviewer) with min occurrence=5; Baseline 2 = Combined Scopus+WoS co-occurrence mapping without topic modeling; Proposed pipeline = Combined Scopus+WoS + co-citation & co-authorship networks + dynamic topic modeling (BERTopic or dynamic LDA) with temporal windows (2-year sliding windows). Preprocessing: standardize metadata, remove non-research document types, author name disambiguation via algorithmic matching, text cleaning (title+abstract). Topic modeling parameters: min topic size=5, embedding model: SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2), cluster minimum similarity=0.2. Network analysis: compute co-citation and keyword co-occurrence graphs, edge threshold by cosine similarity>0.2, community detection via Leiden algorithm. Emergent-theme operational definition: a topic with fewer than 5 documents in period [t-2,t-1] and at least 5 documents in period [t,t+1] within 2-year windows. Evaluation metrics: emergent-theme count per pipeline; topic coherence (c_v and UMass); cluster stability (adjusted Rand index across 100 bootstrap resamples); precision/recall/F1 of emergent-theme detection vs expert-labeled ground truth (expert panel labels emergent topics from a candidate list of 60 topics); statistical comparison: paired t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank if non-normal) on emergent-theme counts between proposed pipeline and each baseline, alpha=0.05. Ablations: (i) remove Web of Science (proposed minus WoS), (ii) remove topic modeling (network only), (iii) replace dynamic topic model with static LDA, (iv) vary min-occurrence threshold (3,5,10). Reproducibility: fixed random seed, run 100 bootstrap samples for stability metrics. Software and resources: Python 3.10, ScientoPy, VOSviewer, BERTopic/ gensim, SBERT embeddings, compute: single-node with 16 CPU cores, 64 GB RAM. Reporting: emergent-theme list, per-topic timelines, coherence scores, significance tests, and ablation results. Risk Factors and Limitations: Database coverage bias: Scopus and WoS omit some regional and non-English outlets, which may underrepresent local cash waqf practice literature. Deduplication and author disambiguation errors: merged or split records can distort counts and networks. Small-sample topic modeling issues: the final deduped corpus (~237 documents) may be too small for stable high-dimensional topic models, reducing topic coherence and increasing variance. Threshold sensitivity: emergent-theme counts depend strongly on min-occurrence and similarity thresholds; results may not generalize across reasonable parameter choices. Temporal resolution limits: two-year windows may conflate gradual trends or miss very recent bursts. Expert validation constraints: limited expert panel size introduces subjectivity and may not provide a comprehensive ground truth. Tool and implementation bias: different topic modeling and embedding choices (BERTopic vs LDA) will yield divergent topics. Generalization limits: pipeline optimized on cash waqf literature may not transfer directly to other subfields of Islamic finance without retuning.
